02.r: Joins the questioners' arrival to what goes before.

03.r: The questioners arrive and approach Jesus.
03.n: An aorist participle, literally 'having come', placed before the main verb 'they say'.

04.n: The present tense in a past narrative, kept here as in the KJV, ASV and YLT.

06.r: A respectful title for a teacher of the law.
06.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the word is given as the rendering of Hebrew רַבִּי, rabbi. The KJV, Geneva and DRC's 'Master' means teacher in older English, not owner; this study keeps 'master' for κύριος.

07.r: They claim to be certain of his character.
07.n: A perfect form with present meaning, as Abbott-Smith notes: 'to have seen or perceived, hence, to know'. The YLT's 'we have known' renders the perfect form literally.

08.r: Introduces what they say they know.

09.r: A man who is what he appears to be and speaks the truth.
09.n: Abbott-Smith derives the word from the verb 'to escape notice', so its root sense is unconcealed, then actual, real. The BSB's 'honest' and the DRC's 'a true speaker' narrow it to speech.

11.r: Adds a second claim about him.

12.r: Negates the concern: no one's opinion weighs on him.

13.r: No one is a matter of concern to him when he teaches.
13.n: An impersonal verb, 'it is a care': Abbott-Smith gives 'to be an object of care, be a care', usually in the third person with a dative of the person. Literally 'there is not a care to you about no one'; the doubled negative strengthens it. The next clause explains it: he does not look at men's faces.

14.r: Jesus, the one who is not concerned.
14.n: A dative, 'to you', with the impersonal verb. English makes 'you' the subject.

15.r: Names what he does not care about.

16.n: Greek says 'no one' after 'not'; English turns the second negative into 'anyone'.

18.r: Gives the reason for the claim before it.

19.r: He does not judge by a person's standing.
19.n: Abbott-Smith's sense 'to perceive, look (at), see'. To look at someone's face is an idiom for being swayed by who he is; the BSB turns the whole clause into 'You are impartial'.

21.r: A person's face, standing for his rank and importance.
21.n: Abbott-Smith's proper sense is 'the face, countenance', and he notes that the Septuagint uses the word chiefly for Hebrew פָּנִים. The KJV, Geneva, DRC and ASV's 'the person' uses an older English sense of person, the role one plays.

22.r: Of human beings, whoever they are.

23.r: Sets what he does against what he does not do.
23.n: Abbott-Smith calls it an adversative particle, stronger than δέ.

24.r: Marks truth as the ground of his teaching.

25.r: He teaches what is really so.
25.n: The noun of 'true' earlier in the verse. With the preposition it means 'truly', 'in accordance with truth'.

26.r: A particular way, the way of God.

27.r: The way of life God requires, which Jesus teaches.
27.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'a way, path, road', and he notes that the Septuagint uses the word chiefly for Hebrew דֶּרֶךְ.

28.r: Greek puts the article before 'God'; English does not.

29.r: The way that belongs to God.

31.r: Asks whether the payment is permitted.
31.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'it is permitted, lawful' and lists this verse.

32.n: The plain verb 'give', as in Matthew 22:17 on this page. The BSB's 'to pay' is a fair sense but hides the wording.

33.r: The tax levied on each person, owed to Rome.
33.n: Abbott-Smith defines it as 'a poll-tax', from the Latin census, and lists this verse, noting that one edition's margin reads ἐπικεφάλαιον here, a word for a tax by head. The older translations' 'tribute' is kept in this study for φόρος.

34.r: To the Roman emperor, the one the tax is paid to.

35.r: Sets up the two answers, yes or no.

36.r: The second alternative: it is not lawful.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus opens with οἱ δὲ ἐλθόντες, 'and they, having come', using the article as a pronoun and δέ in place of καί, and it places 'to give' elsewhere in the question. The sense is unchanged, and the KJV's 'And when they were come' and 'to give tribute' read the same either way.
